title: Find Peak Element
statement:
A **peak** of an array is an element that is strictly greater than each of its neighbours. The first element only has a right neighbour and the last element only has a left neighbour; treat the positions just outside the array as holding negative infinity, so the first element is a peak if it is greater than the second, and the last element is a peak if it is greater than the one before it. An array of one element is a peak by itself.

You are given an array of `n` distinct integers that is a **mountain**: it is strictly increasing up to some index and strictly decreasing after it. Either side may be empty, so a strictly increasing or strictly decreasing array is also a mountain. A mountain has exactly one peak.

Print the **0-based index** of the peak.

Reading every element takes `O(n)`. The interviewers who asked this problem expected a solution that inspects only `O(log n)` elements of the array by using binary search; your program still has to read the input, but design the search itself with that bound in mind.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers: the array.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the index of the peak.
constraints: The array is strictly increasing up to one index and strictly decreasing after it (all values are distinct)

examples.explanation: The values rise 1, 4, 9 and then fall 7, 2. The peak 9 is at index 2.
The array only increases, so the last element is the peak: 11 is greater than its left neighbour 8.
The array only decreases, so the first element is the peak.

hints: Compare a middle element with its right neighbour. What does that comparison say about which side of the middle the peak is on?
If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] you are on the rising slope, so the peak is strictly to the right. Otherwise the peak is at mid or to its left.
Keep a range [lo, hi] that always contains the peak. Stop when it shrinks to one index; no special case for the array ends is needed.

def gen(rng):
    def mountain(n, p, hi=1000000):
        vals = rng.sample(range(0, hi + 1), n)
        vals.sort()
        top = vals.pop()
        rng.shuffle(vals)
        left = sorted(vals[:p])
        right = sorted(vals[p:], reverse=True)
        return left + [top] + right
    def fmt(a):
        return f'{len(a)}\n' + ' '.join(map(str, a))
    tests = [fmt([5]), fmt([1, 2]), fmt([2, 1]), fmt([1, 3, 2]), fmt([0, 1000000])]
    for _ in range(9):
        n = rng.randint(1, 30)
        tests.append(fmt(mountain(n, rng.randint(0, n - 1), 99)))
    N = 100000
    tests.append(fmt(mountain(N, 0)))
    tests.append(fmt(mountain(N, N - 1)))
    tests.append(fmt(mountain(N, N // 2)))
    tests.append(fmt(mountain(N, rng.randint(1, N - 2))))
    tests.append(fmt(mountain(N, 31337)))
    return tests
